bibliography.abstract: Extreme rainfall can rapidly degrade road-network functionality (RNF), disrupting emergency mobility, accessibility, evacuation, logistics, and infrastructure restoration. Existing flood-transportation impact models are often difficult to deploy across regions because they rely on local calibration, intensive simulation workflows or target-region retraining. This study proposes G-R2R, a transferable spatiotemporal graph-learning framework that reframes rainfall-induced road-network disruption as a region-conditioned, topology-flexible graph forecasting problem for unseen transportation networks. The framework integrates ego-centered subgraph sampling, terrain-conditioned graph representation, region-conditioned dual-level static encoding, and dynamic rainfall-network feature learning. Static geographic and infrastructure attributes are fused with rainfall forcing and recent RNF states to forecast node-level RNF across heterogeneous road networks. G-R2R is evaluated using simulation-derived RNF sequences from ten flood-prone regions in Wenzhou, China, under unseen-region testing protocols. It outperforms representative forecasting baselines, achieving a stabilized MAPE of 2.33% and $R^2$ of 0.855 under the fixed unseen-region benchmark. Leave-one-area-out evaluation yields stabilized MAPE values of 2.30%-3.54%. Ablation analysis supports the contributions of the terrain-conditioned graph representation and dual-level static encoding. A historical-event replay of Typhoon Fitow further shows that G-R2R reproduces principal temporal trajectories and node-level spatial patterns of the simulation-derived RNF reference under observed rainfall forcing without target-region retraining. These results support rapid and transferable node-level RNF forecasting across the regional road-network domains represented in this study.
bibliography.title: From Rainfall to Road-Network Functionality: Transferable Graph Forecasting for Flood-Disrupted Transportation Networks

en.caveats: The model was evaluated against simulated network functionality data from a single municipal region rather than real-world observed road closures.
en.what: G-R2R, a transferable spatiotemporal graph-learning framework, forecasts node-level road-network functionality during extreme rainfall across unseen transportation networks without target-region retraining. The model integrates subgraph sampling, dynamic rainfall forcing, terrain conditions, and static dual-level encodings, and was evaluated on simulation-derived sequences from ten flood-prone regions in Wenzhou, China. It achieved a Mean Absolute Percentage Error of 2.33% and an R² of 0.855 under unseen-region benchmarks, while reproducing temporal trajectories and spatial patterns during a historical replay of Typhoon Fitow.
en.why: Disruption models can now predict road network degradation in completely uncalibrated regions immediately during extreme rainfall events, bypassing computationally intensive simulations and local data calibration.
